title: Latency surgery: quant kernel rescue notes
body:
Context:
This is a rough labbook of a targeted investigation we ran after recurring 99p tail spikes for INT8/AWQ model shards on the prod-like perf cluster (a3x2 nodes, mixed V100/RTX8k-equivalent). Goal: isolate kernel-level sources of tail latency amplification during mixed small/long requests and produce immediate mitigations we can ship as config knobs for Dedicated and Hosted routes.

Short summary (executive):
- Reproduced 99.9p tail with synthetic mixed workload (80% short prompts ~32 tokens, 20% long ~2048 tokens) using the replay harness.
- Two dominant contributors to tail: (1) KV cache miss amplification at sequence boundaries, (2) kernel occupancy imbalance for AWQ packing kernels causing GPU-side serialization under multi-tenant multiplexing.
- Quick mitigations validated: prefix coalescing (server-side) reduced tail by ~28% on the mix; adaptive kernel pre-warming for AWQ improved 99p by ~18% and 99.9p by ~24%.
- Longer term: expose kernel packing thresholds, improve prefetch heuristics, and add a scheduler soft quota that favors ongoing long-context workers to reduce interference.

Environment & harness:
- Hardware: test cluster with homogeneous A100 equivalent, 40GB; secondary experiments on an older V100 rack to check cross-arch effects.
- Software: runtime revision rtd-2026-04-peak, kernels branch awq-multipack-v2, pytorch 2.1 fork for fused ops, CUDA 11.8.
- Models: LLAMA-variant 13B converted to AWQ/GPTQ/INT8/FP8 variants using our standard quant pipeline.
- Workload driver: replay harness with poisson arrivals, target concurrency 40, adjustable short/long ratio. Instrumentation: per-call tracing (client->router->executor), nvprof-style kernel timing traces, and in-GPU counters for SM occupancy, warp stalls, and shared memory utilization.

Methodology notes (quick checklist we used):
- Start with single-tenant baseline for each quant type (AWQ, GPTQ, INT8, FP8).
- Run isolation microbench (single request at 40 concurrency) to gather kernel timing distribution (mean/99/99.9).
- Introduce mixed client patterns to reproduce tail.
- Capture flamegraphs at kernel level, plus GPU counters for offending samples (above 99.5p).
- Inject targeted mitigations (prefix coalesce, pre-warm cache, kernel prefetch) one at a time.
- Repeat under slight cross-tenant interference to validate robustness.

Key observations (detailed):
1) KV cache miss amplification:
- When long requests finish, the executor drops partial KV pages and then reads them back for subsequent requests; in our trace the cost of re-building the KV slices across many small concurrent tasks created a serialized hotspot on the memcpy+deserialize path.
- Metrics: average extra memcpy time per miss ~0.8ms on A100, but at tail this amplifies to 6-12ms due to queued host->device memcpy and driver serialization under high concurrency.
- Workaround tested: prefix coalescing that groups small requests sharing a recent prefix into a single KV slice build reduced the number of rebuilds by ~65% in the mixed workload and dropped 99.9p by ~22%.

2) AWQ kernel occupancy imbalance and packing jitter:
- AWQ packing kernel has two execution paths: vectorized fast path (for aligned blocks) and fallback scalar path that is ~3-4x slower. Corner-case token alignments (seen frequently with long-context boundaries) cause many warps to take the fallback path, which creates head-of-line stalls for other cooperative kernels on the same SMs.
- Traces show the fallback path has high shared-memory contention and a 2-3x increase in warp-stall reasons 'sync' and 'mem'.
- Under multiplexing with other tenants (even best-effort), these stalls cascade: a slow warp holds a tail of descriptors and prevents subsequent kernels from launching promptly. We measured a median kernel launch latency increase of 0.6ms and a 99.9p surge of 9-15ms correlated with fallback path entries.

3) Scheduler preemption jitter:
- Our in-GPU scheduler favors small kernels and can preempt larger in-progress transforms in busy states, but preemption causes a resume penalty (observed ~2–4ms) that shows up disproportionately for long-context requests when they intersect with bursts of short requests.
- Mitigation: a soft reservation for long-running kernels (TTL per-stream) reduces preemption without starving short jobs; this lowered 99p by ~12% in the experiment.

Micro-experiment results (representative numbers):
- Baseline (mixed, no mitigations):  p50 12.4ms, p95 38.1ms, p99 96.2ms, p99.9 214.7ms.
- Add prefix coalescing: p50 11.9ms, p95 34.0ms, p99 82.9ms, p99.9 167.3ms.
- Add AWQ kernel pre-warm (compile-and-cache path primed for common alignments): p50 11.6ms, p95 31.8ms, p99 75.2ms, p99.9 128.1ms.
- All mitigations combined + scheduler soft reservation: p50 11.1ms, p95 30.7ms, p99 68.4ms, p99.9 102.5ms.
Notes: absolute numbers vary by node generation; these are A100-equivalent runs.

Deviations by quant type:
- INT8: generally lower mean latency but larger variance when vectorized kernels drop to fallback; INT8 fallback penalties are similar magnitude to AWQ but slightly less frequent because packing alignment differs.
- GPTQ: more stable launch patterns, but KV spine rebuilds were costlier because GPTQ's decode path uses additional host-side packing; adding a fused serialize path helped.
- FP8: higher per-token compute time but fewer small-kernel fallbacks, so tail is more influenced by scheduling and memcpy than packing.

Actionable mitigations (immediate ship candidates):
- Server-side prefix coalescer (config off by default, opt-in per-route) to reduce redundant KV rebuilds.
- Kernel pre-warm path that pre-compiles/allocates AWQ-aligned buffers for common token alignment signatures. Expose knob to increase pre-warm budget for routes with long-context mix.
- Scheduler soft reservation parameter to reduce preemption of long-running kernels; default conservative value validated in test harness.
- Metric improvements: add per-route counters for 'fallback-path-entry' and 'kv-rebuilds' so we can alert on patterns that historically lead to tail spikes.

Follow-ups and open questions:
- Need deeper root-cause on why certain token alignment signatures cluster in real traffic — is it a client-side encoder artifact? Should we normalize alignment at the router?
- Explore a lightweight GPU-side KV cache persistence across short-lived tasks to avoid host->device round-trip for very hot prefixes. Risks: memory pressure and eviction complexity.
- Quant-specific kernel rewrite: can we reduce fallback penalty by making the packing kernel more tolerant to misalignment (at cost of some throughput)? A hybrid microkernel was sketched in a spike but needs engineering validation.

Notes to later self / handoff:
- Samir: follow up on kernel pre-warm config and a small API to expose alignment signatures from the model loader.
- Lina: add the two counters to telemetry pipeline and create an alert runbook.
- Marcus: spike on GPU-side persistent KV cache prototype and estimate RAM and eviction overhead for Dedicated pools.

Appendix (quick commands we used):
- run harness: ./tools/replay --profile=quant-latency-surgery --concurrency=40 --mix=80:20 --model=13B-awq --nodes=3
- collect traces: ./tools/collect-trace --run=quant-latency-surgery --nvprof --gpu-counters=sm_efficiency,shared_load,warp_stalls
- flamegraph extraction: ./tools/flame --input trace.json --level kernel --threshold 0.001

End of notes. This doc is intentionally informal; will convert to a PRD if we decide on roadmap changes.
